To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the application of nitrogen fertilizer increased the nitrate leaching from white clover/grass pastures, and increased the nitrate-N concentration of groundwater under the pastures.

Nitrogen fertilizer applications up to 400 kg N/ha/year to dairy pastures can increase nitrate-N leaching to groundwater by up to 4-fold, and increase nitrous oxide emissions from soil by up to 5 fold, compared to pastures with no nitrogen fertilizer.

1) the nitrogen fertilizer rate of 0.4 kg N ha - 1 year -1 is equivalent to the nitrogen input from urine and dung deposited by a dairy cow on pasture, and 2) the nitrate-N leaching losses are 1.5-3 times higher than from a pasture grazed by a cow, when the same rate of nitrogen fertilizer is applied.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following issues.
the environmental implications of different nitrogen inputs to pasture on dairy farms.
the environmental impacts of dairy farming, and in particular, with nitrate leaching and groundwater pollution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the environmental impacts of dairy farming in New Zealand are not as great as those in many other countries, but that they are not insignificant and need to be carefully monitored.
the nitrogen losses from the average New Zealand dairy farm are similar to those in Europe, but the nitrate leaching is greater.

the average dairy farm in New Zealand is unlikely to cause environmental damage from nitrate leaching, but the risk of this occurring is greater for some farms, particularly those on poorly drained soils and those with high nitrogen inputs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the environmental impact of dairy farming in New Zealand is small, but that there are some opportunities for further improvement.
nitrogen losses were small in relation to the amount of nitrogen applied and the nitrogen fertilizer rates used were well within the range used by farmers.
, in the absence of nitrogen fertilizer, nitrate leaching from grazed pastures was low, but increased with nitrogen fertilizer application and the amount of nitrogen in the diet of dairy cows.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the nitrogen losses are very much greater than those that are typically reported for New Zealand farms and are similar to those from European countries where losses are typically higher than in New Zealand.
the nitrogen fertilizer rates used on the 200 and 400 N farmlets were not sustainable for a dairy system in New Zealand, because of the large losses of nitrogen to groundwater.
the Resource Management Act is not fit for purpose for managing the environmental impacts of nitrogen inputs on dairy farm.
